lessons.title: Comparing
intro: FORTRAN IV (1962) added a second IF: IF (condition) statement. If the condition is true, the one statement after it runs. If not, the computer goes on to the next card.
Comparisons are written with dots: .LT. (less than), .LE. (less or equal), .EQ. (equal), .NE. (not equal), .GT. (greater), .GE. (greater or equal).
Why the dots? The IBM keypunch had no < or > keys. Letters between dots were the way to write them.

exercises.explanation: G for greater, E for equal: .GE. is ≥.

exercises.prompt: Why does FORTRAN write .GT. instead of >?
options: The keypunch had no < and > keys
exercises.explanation: Programs were punched on machines like the IBM 026, and its keyboard had no such signs.

exercises.prompt: Print ZERO when N is zero.

exercises.explanation: K is 3, so K .LT. 10 is true and the first WRITE runs. K .GE. 10 is false, so the second one is skipped.

exercises.prompt: This job stops with *ERROR*. Which card is wrong?
exercises.explanation: FORTRAN IV doesn't know >. Write X .GT. 0.0.

exercises.prompt: How many statements can follow a logical IF?
options: As many as fit on the card
None, it must be a jump
exercises.explanation: IF (condition) statement: one statement, often a GO TO when more needs to happen.

lessons.title: AND, OR, NOT
intro: Conditions can be combined: .AND. is true when both sides are true, .OR. when at least one is, and .NOT. turns true into false and back.
IF (I .GE. 10 .AND. I .LE. 20) checks whether I lies between 10 and 20. Comparisons are worked out first, then .NOT., then .AND., then .OR.
MOD(A, B) gives the remainder of A divided by B. MOD(Y, 4) .EQ. 0 asks: can Y be divided by 4?

options: When at least one is true
When at least one is true
Only when exactly one is true

exercises.prompt: Print WEEKEND when D is 6 or 7.
exercises.explanation: A day can't be 6 and 7 at once, so it must be .OR. And without the dots, FORTRAN wouldn't recognize it.
MOD(7, 2) is 1, so MOD(N, 2) .EQ. 0 is false, and .NOT. makes it true.

exercises.prompt: This job stops with *ERROR*. Which card is wrong?

lessons.title: IF and GO TO
intro: A logical IF runs just one statement. To do more, make that statement a GO TO: IF (N .GE. 90) GO TO 10 jumps to a whole block of cards.
A chain of IF … GO TO checks one condition after the other. The order matters: check 90 before 60, or a score of 95 would stop at "60 or more".
Every block ends with GO TO to a common card, so only one of them runs.

exercises.prompt: In the example, what does N = 95 print?
exercises.explanation: 95 .GE. 90 is true, so it jumps to 10 and prints TOP. GO TO 40 skips the rest.
Neither IF is true, so the computer reads on to the WRITE that prints FAIL.

exercises.prompt: Why must IF (N .GE. 90) come before IF (N .GE. 60)?
options: Otherwise 95 would jump to PASS, because 95 is also 60 or more
FORTRAN reads IFs from the bottom up
Bigger numbers must come first in a deck
exercises.explanation: The first true condition wins. Check the strictest one first.

exercises.prompt: Jump to 50 when X is negative.
exercises.explanation: The statement after a logical IF can be a GO TO.

exercises.prompt: Stack the cards: print BIG when K is over 100, otherwise SMALL.
exercises.explanation: The IF jumps over the SMALL block. GO TO 30 keeps SMALL from running into BIG.

exercises.prompt: With N = 75 this prints PASS and then TOP. Which card is wrong?
exercises.explanation: After printing PASS, the computer falls through to card 10. That WRITE needs a GO TO after it, or the PASS card should jump past TOP.
